Finally, we encounter the stars especially assigned to minerals, metals, and gemstones, which are divided according to the nature of the minerals and the order of the planets. Therefore, some are called Antimonial, others Vitriolic, others Sulfurous, others Arsenical, others Mercurial stars, etc., which through their harmful and poisonous dissolutions are accustomed to poison the air and the water and to cause regional plagues. Thus it is said that the Solar stars, through their ejections soaked with the three principles <note>Salt, Sulfur, Mercury</note>, first and foremost bear the carbuncles and jaspers, but subsequently the Indian or most solid gold. The Lunar stars bear the sapphires and solid silver; the Martial stars bear the rubies and iron; the Jovial stars bear the white sapphires and tin; the stars subject to the domain of Venus bear the emeralds and copper; the Mercurial stars work the hyacinths and quicksilver; the Saturnine stars bring forth from the heaven also the crystals, beryls, diamonds, and lead.

Paracelsus explains these astronomical secrets in Volume 2, page 35 C, thus: "In the same way, there are also other stars that eject from themselves gems and garnets and other forms of stones. For the Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt in the element of Fire are powerful in the birth of gems. There are many stars that stand in the Rubinic Sulfur, many in the Sapphiric Salt, many in the Emeraldic Mercury, etc."

Also in the same place, page 36 A: "As an emerald is a copper-stone, a carbuncle or jasper is a gold-stone, a ruby and chalcedony is an iron-stone, a blue sapphire is a silver-stone, a white sapphire is a stone of Jupiter, a hyacinth is a stone of Mercury. Schrift zum Grunde gelegt werden müßte, nämlich, daß jeder einzelne geschriebene Laut der fremden Schrift durch einen einzigen leicht verständlichen und allgemein anwendbaren Buchstaben ausgedrückt wird. Hierbei habe ich möglichst die in linguistischen Büchern schon sehr allgemein aufgenommenen Bezeichnungen beibehalten und schreibe z. B. für 𓊪𓊪𓊪 oder 𓊪𓊪, kopt. ϣ, nicht *sch* oder *sh* oder *ch*, sondern *ś*, für den erweichten Guttural, der im Koptischen durch das besondere Zeichen ϧ ausgedrückt wird *ǵ*. Die meiste Schwierigkeit hat bisher immer die Bezeichnung der gutturalen Spirans dargeboten, welche im Deutschen durch *ch*, im Spanischen durch *x* oder *j* ausgedrückt wird. Dieser Laut erscheint auch im hieroglyphischen Alphabete als 𓐍 oder 𓐎, kopt. ϧ. Er wurde bisher meistens durch *ch* oder *kh*, also durch zwei Zeichen ausgedrückt, von denen das erste sogar einen nicht vorhandenen Gaumenschluß voraussetzt. Dies ist schon prinzipmäßig entschieden zurückzuweisen; es führt aber auch leicht zu Mißverständnissen, da man z. B. die hieroglyphischen Gruppen 𓂋𓐍𓎛 und 𓂋𓐍 beide durch *rekh* umschreiben müßte, während die Buchstaben offenbar nur auf die letztere Gruppe, kopt. ⲣⲱϩ, passen; ebenso könnte man im Königsnamen <insert>𓇳𓏠𓈖𓇳𓏠𓈖</insert> *Sebekhotep*, den die Griechen *Σεβεχώπις* gesprochen haben würden, zweifeln, ob das *h* zu dem vorausgehenden *k*, oder, wie es richtig ist, zu dem folgenden Vokale zu ziehen wäre. Mir scheint nach Erwägung aller Umstände für den einfachen Laut des deutschen *ch* kein passenderes Zeichen gefunden werden zu können, als das griechische *χ*, welches wir dafür festhalten. Im Arabischen steht der harten Aspirate *خ*, die entsprechende schwache *غ* zur Seite, welche sich zur ersteren genau wie *g* zu *k* unter den mutis verhält, und deshalb auch gewöhnlich durch *gh*, wie jene durch *kh* ausgedrückt wird. Für uns läßt sich ein und derselbe Grundlaut auch nur durch dasselbe Zeichen *χ* ausdrücken, dessen starke Form durch einen *spiritus asper* *χ̔*, die schwache durch einen *lenis* *χ̓* unterschieden wird, wie *ś* das französische *ch*, *ś* das französische *j*, oder wie *ġ* das arabische *غ*, *g* das *ج* bezeichnet. Eine andere große Schwierigkeit bei der Umschrift der Hieroglyphen ist der häufige Mangel der Vokale. Die Aegypter pflegten früher nur die drei Grundvokale zu schreiben 𓇋, 𓂝 oder 𓄿 für *a*, 𓇋𓇋 oder 𓇋 für *i*

namely, that every single written sound of the foreign script is expressed by a single, easily understandable, and universally applicable letter. In doing so, I have kept as much as possible to the designations already very generally accepted in linguistic books and write, for example, for 𓊪𓊪𓊪 or 𓊪𓊪, Coptic ϣ, not *sch* or *sh* or *ch*, but *ś*; for the softened guttural, which is expressed in Coptic by the special sign ϧ, I write *ǵ*. Most of the difficulty has hitherto always been presented by the designation of the guttural spirant, which is expressed in German by *ch*, in Spanish by *x* or *j*. This sound also appears in the hieroglyphic alphabet as 𓐍 or 𓐎, Coptic ϧ. It was hitherto mostly expressed by *ch* or *kh*, i.e., by two signs, the first of which even presupposes a palatal closure that does not exist. This is to be rejected on principle; but it also easily leads to misunderstandings, since, for example, one would have to transcribe the hieroglyphic groups 𓂋𓐍𓎛 and 𓂋𓐍 both as *rekh*, while the letters clearly only fit the latter group, Coptic ⲣⲱϩ; likewise, one could doubt in the royal name <insert>𓇳𓏠𓈖𓇳𓏠𓈖</insert> *Sebekhotep*, which the Greeks would have pronounced as *Sebekhōpis*, whether the *h* should be drawn to the preceding *k*, or, as is correct, to the following vowel. After considering all circumstances, there seems to me no more suitable sign for the simple sound of the German *ch* than the Greek *χ*, which we retain for this purpose. In Arabic, the hard aspirate *خ* is accompanied by the corresponding weak *غ*, which relates to the former exactly as *g* relates to *k* among the mutae <note>linguistic term for plosive consonants</note>, and is therefore also usually expressed by *gh*, just as the former is by *kh*. For us, one and the same root sound can also only be expressed by the same sign *χ*, whose strong form is distinguished by a *spiritus asper* *χ̔*, the weak by a *lenis* *χ̓*, just as *ś* denotes the French *ch*, *ś* the French *j*, or as *ġ* denotes the Arabic *غ*, *g* the *ج*. Another great difficulty in the transcription of hieroglyphs is the frequent lack of vowels. The Egyptians usually only wrote the three basic vowels 𓇋, 𓂝, or 𓄿 for *a*, 𓇋𓇋 or 𓇋 for *i*

100. If one wants to be a devil, then God’s wrath will have him, for he is of his property; the choice is soon made. But if he wants to be an angel, then the chooser is soon there as well.

101. But if he has been an evil man, and God’s wrath has already chosen him for damnation, yet he lets the little spark of the love of God into the light of life—which is possible without this, while the outer man stands against him and calls to him—then the chooser for the Kingdom of Heaven is also immediately in that same little spark, and with it, with very great joy and honor, [greater] than [over] ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.

102. The soul of man is from the center that is called God the Father; understand, from the eternal, unbegun nature. It has the center for fire and light within itself, for evil and good. What it chooses for itself, by that same thing it is chosen and received again; which can be seen in the devils.

103. They were angels in God’s light, and their center moved itself even higher than is the right of the angelic nature, and they awakened in themselves the mother of the primordial state in ferocity; that [ferocity] also immediately caught their spirit-will and chose them as creatures of the dark world.

104. Do you think now that it was God’s predetermining will? Then God would have to have a devil’s will in himself, and also an angelic one; that would be entirely against the Scripture of the Saints, also against God’s love, and against the light of the eternal nature.

105. But the Lampoon understands nothing of what God’s love and wrath is, what God is called. He wants to speak of God’s will, and it is only shadow-boxing and jugglery.

106. But because he does not understand it, and I see his miserable blindness by the grace of God, how he burns in the poison of the primordial state, and thus gives a proper advocate to the wrath of God, as well as to the devil, to imprison and keep the poor souls in God’s wrath, I will reveal it to him somewhat. If he wants to buy now, very well; then let Immanuel be ours, and the devil [the property] of the dark world.

107. But if he does not want to, then I have made it for the reader of his lampoon, so he will be able to judge us well in his mind and understanding; it shall be a one-time defense.

Es giebt zweyerley Leute, die da schweigen; einige, weil sie nichts zu reden haben, andere aber weil sie dessen allzuviel haben: eben so ist es auch in diesem Grad des Gebets; man schweiget vor lauter Ueberfluß, und nicht aus Mangel. Das Wasser bringet zweyerley Personen den Tod; aber auf ganz verschiedene Weise: der eine stirbt vor Durst, der andere ersäuft; der eine stirbt aus Mangel, der andere aus Ueberfluß. Alhier macht es der Ueberfluß, daß die Wirkungen aufhören.

Es hat demnach in diesem Grade vieles auf sich: daß man, so viel als nur immer möglich ist, im Stillschweigen verharre. Just so it is also here: the creature no longer distinguishes and notices its activity; because a very bright and general light swallows all the small distinct lights and completely obscures them; because its exceedingly great clarity surpasses them all.

So I say then, that this inability to act comes not from lack, but from abundance; as he who will make a trial of it will easily distinguish: such a person will recognize that it is not an unfruitful silence caused by lack; but a full and unction-rich silence that comes from pure abundance. There are two kinds of people who are silent; some because they have nothing to say, but others because they have all too much: just so it is also in this degree of prayer; one is silent out of pure abundance, and not out of lack. Water brings death to two kinds of persons; but in quite different ways: one dies of thirst, the other drowns; one dies from lack, the other from abundance. Here it is abundance that makes the activities cease.

In this degree, much depends on this: that one remains in silence as much as is ever possible. External silence is very necessary to maintain inner stillness: and it is impossible to become a truly inward person where one does not love silence and solitude. <term>GOTT</term> <gloss>God</gloss> says it to us through the mouth of his prophet: I will lead her into the wilderness or solitude, and there speak to her heart.

<margin>Omnipotence.</margin>
<margin>Chapter 13 <note>Likely referring to a specific chapter in Arndt's True Christianity</note></margin>
...God's omnipotence, for we know that God is higher, mightier, and stronger than all the misfortune of this world, than sin, death, the devil, and hell. Therefore, Psalm 46:1 states: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in the great troubles that have befallen us. Therefore, we do not fear, even if the world should pass away. Hence also the holy Job says: Though the Lord should kill me, yet I will hope in Him <note>Job 13:15</note>. This is as if he were to say: He can certainly make me alive again. Abraham thought the same when he was to sacrifice his son: God can certainly make him alive again. Indeed, God's omnipotence is before our eyes daily in the great structure of heaven and earth. What do you see when you look at heaven and earth? God's omnipotence, of which the prophet Isaiah speaks in 40:12 and following: Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and marked off the heavens with a span, and enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance, and directed the Spirit of the Lord, or who has instructed Him? Behold, the nations are like a drop in a bucket, and are counted as the small dust on the scales; the islands are like a speck of dust; all nations are as nothing and as vanity. From this you should conclude: if God can maintain the great structure of heaven and earth, and such great, mighty nations, then He will certainly also maintain you, who are but a small speck of dust of the earth. To this end, Psalm 104:5 and following praises the work of creation, and sets before our eyes heaven, earth, sea, and all creatures, showing how God maintains and nourishes them. And Psalm 135:5 and following: I know that the Lord is great, and our Lord is above all gods; whatever He pleases, He does in heaven, on earth, in the seas, and in all deeps. He causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth; He makes lightning with the rain; He brings the wind out of His secret treasuries. Lord, You have founded heaven and earth by Your great power and outstretched arm, and nothing is impossible for You, You great and mighty God, Lord of Sabaoth <term>Zebaoth</term> <gloss>Hosts</gloss> is Your name. Great in counsel and mighty in deed <note>Jeremiah 32:17-19</note>. All of nature is full of this testimony of God's omnipotence, which Job also magnificently describes in his 38th chapter. We should look upon this and thereby dampen our unbelief.

<margin>5. Fervent Prayer.</margin>
The fifth remedy for our unbelief is prayer: "Ah, Lord, increase our faith" <note>Luke 17:5</note>. Mark 9:24: "Lord, I believe; help my unbelief!" Watch and pray that you do not fall into temptation. We carry our treasure in earthen vessels <note>2 Corinthians 4:7</note>. Psalm 119:80: "Let my heart be blameless in Your statutes, that I may not be put to shame," and do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth. Psalm 86:11: "Teach me Your way, O Lord, that I may walk in Your truth; unite my heart to fear Your name."

<margin>6. God's Gracious Presence.</margin>
Upon such prayer follows God's gracious presence, which should comfort us more than the world with all its power can terrify us. As Saint John says in 1 John 4:4: "He who is in us is greater than he who is in the world." Psalm 56:4: "In God I will hope and not be afraid; what can flesh do to me?" Psalm 27:1: "The Lord is my light and my salvation," for He covers me in His pavilion in the evil time. Proverbs 18:10: "The name of the Lord is a strong tower." For this reason Joshua also speaks in Numbers 14:9: "The Lord is with us; do not fear the great people; their protection has departed from them." Isaiah 41:10 and 43:1-2: "Fear not, I am with you; do not be dismayed, I am your God; I strengthen, rescue, and help you through the right hand of My righteousness. When you pass through fire and water, I am with you, so that the streams shall not drown you, nor the flame ignite you." Psalm 91:15: "I am with him in trouble." Psalm 77:19: "Your way was in the sea, and Your path in great waters, and yet no one perceived Your

<column-break/>

footprints." Thus God is often with us without us noticing it. Through this we should come to the aid of our unbelief, for we could not live for a single moment without God or outside of God. By this even the ungodly are convinced that the Lord God means well by them and would gladly convert them, because He preserves them in life and does them much good out of overflowing mercy. For in God we live, move, and have our being <note>Acts 17:28</note>. How much more does He want those who fear God to learn to trust Him from the heart, and to let go of all unbelief, and rather surrender themselves to Him entirely.

<margin>7. Punishment of Unbelief.</margin>
7. We should consider the terrible, irreparable fall that arises from unbelief, and the Psalm recounts three gruesome fruits of unbelief. 1. Contempt for God. 2. Murmuring or blasphemy against God. 3. Disobedience. Upon these the terrible punishment follows, that God wished to destroy them. By this God has indicated that the despisers of God, the blasphemers, and the disobedient are worthy of neither temporal nor eternal life. For this reason, the scouts of the promised land, who made the people unbelieving and disobedient, had to die before their eyes. Indeed, all the children of Israel who had become unbelieving, from twenty years old and upward, had to die in the wilderness and did not enter the promised land, except for Joshua and Caleb. This signifies that whoever despises the heavenly fatherland through unbelief will not enter it. Just as those who despised the heavenly invitation were not worthy to taste God's supper <note>referring to the Parable of the Great Banquet</note>.

<margin>Luke 14:24</margin>
<margin>8. Examples of the Saints.</margin>
8. Look also at the examples of the saints, whom unbelief also greatly plagued at times. I hold that Abraham, Moses, Joshua, David, and Elijah were likely the strongest-believing men in the world, yet unbelief plagued them at times. Abraham, the father of all believers, was plagued by unbelief so that he feared he would lose his life, even though God had often spoken to him and told him his seed should become like the stars in heaven. Therefore, Abraham denied his wife twice and said she was his sister; once in Egypt <note>Genesis 12:11 and following</note> and the other time at Gerar with King Abimelech, for Sarah was a beautiful woman, and Abraham thought they would murder him and take his wife. Moses fell into great unbelief in Numbers 11:21 and following. When God commanded him to give the people meat, he said: there are six hundred thousand men here, and You say, give them meat? And although those who are not able to perform such a task skillfully can neither be compelled to undertake it, nor be held in contempt, so much the less can it be turned into a vice and a crime if some acknowledge a lack of that exquisite training and do not boast or gloriously show themselves off when the deed does not correspond to their opinion and posturing. Hence, the blessed B. Bohnius in *Examination of Lethal Wounds* <note>original: "Exam. vuln. lethal."</note>, sect. 1, ch. 1, p. 10, says: "I praise the prudence of those who, measuring themselves by their own yardstick and knowing that they are not sufficiently trained in conducting autopsies, modestly decline the task of cutting, inspecting, and testifying here, even if requested." Just as that prudence is to be commended in forensic medicine so that this <term>intexav</term> <gloss>the act of weaving together/connecting [evidence]</gloss> is properly exercised, so too must the physician occasionally abstain out of conscience, lest he hide the truth and, for a less than honest reason, suspend his judgment and abstain from speaking the truth. And since, in this forum of legal medicine, the practitioner must proceed circumspectly regarding every single circumstance, he should also bring forth solid reasons with which to bolster his abstention from judging, lest any incompetence, timidity, negligence, or foolishness be imputed to him. Therefore, we have so far indicated the prudent abstention of the physician from the sick and from various intricate cases. In this place, we touch briefly upon that dangerous case when a medical practitioner is called to women in childbirth who have been brought into extreme danger of life by unskilled midwives and women who think themselves wise beyond the sphere of their sex, and it is implicitly offered to him to improve what others have made worse. In this case, an opportunity sometimes shines upon the prudent practitioner to exercise abstention, lest he take the blame for the actions of those preceding him and submit himself to unjust judgments. For such intricate and delicate cases are ones that can easily bring disgrace instead of glory. And although in such depraved cases, he must sometimes deny his positive aid and duty, the prudent physician can, out of his remaining sincerity and sound sense, indicate what is to be hoped for or feared, or in what cause the danger and difficulty lie.

<margin>The Book of Thoth. (Theater of Wonders. 14.)</margin>

My readers will, by now, be saturated with wonders, if not with horror, and it is time that I bring this book to an end. Even if I have achieved nothing else, I hope at least to have contributed something to your entertainment; although I would be pleased to learn that I have caused some, or even just one, to view life and death, along with the secrets attached to both, with a more searching gaze than they were previously accustomed to. I cannot help but think it would be a great step forward for the human race if it could become familiar with the idea that we are spirits who only wear an armor of flesh for a while. The loosening of the bond between soul and body, although it changes the outward movements of the former, leaves its moral core unchanged. What a person has made of themselves, that they shall be; their condition is the result of their past life, and heaven and hell lie within themselves. With death, we enter a new path of life, and its nature depends on us. If we have provided our lamps with oil and are prepared for a noble destiny, for association with the good spirits who have gone before us, then this will be our portion; but if we have abused our talents and immersed our souls in the sensual lusts or base passions of the world, we carry the desire for them over with us; and it will certainly become a torment to us, if it does not perhaps bind us to the earth through unquenchable remorse or frustrated designs, as I have mentioned regarding so many unhappy spirits...

Answer: Herr Primarius! I do not lead people away from the preached and written Word; you do me injustice in that case. But I say that they should bring the temple of Jesus Christ to the preached or written word, as a repentant, hungry soul, which hears Christ, as the living Word, teaching within itself in the literal and preached word, as David says: "I will hear what the Lord speaks in me," and Christ also said: "Whoever is from God hears God’s Word." And to the Pharisees, He said: "Therefore you do not hear, for you are not from God." Likewise: "You are not my sheep." So it is my opinion that a human must have divine ears (as a repentant soul) when he wishes to hear Christ’s voice, be it in the sermon, in reading, or speaking; for such has Christ taught us, Him I believe more than all art. For historical faith with knowledge, tickling, and consolation, without power and earnest will, is dead and only a husk, and does not reach sonship; it must be earnest. Herr Primarius, it is not enough that we go to church and to the sacrament and sit there for an hour and look pious and hear a sermon, where often stubble and wheat are sown together among you, in that you sometimes slander so. No: Church-going profits no one anything unless he hears the Word of God in the church actually in his soul. Since it is not the office of women to instruct others, but rather to be instructed by others, as St. Paul writes, it is easy to see that it is a new miracle that a weak woman was so magnanimous that she dared to undertake such a great matter. She was so witty and strong that she was able to bring it to an end, stealing the hearts of those with whom she associated so that she might lead them to God, drawing so many after her toward everything that is contrary to the senses of man. In my opinion, however, Almighty God in these times (when the evil enemy triumphs, as it were, in the multitude of so many unbelievers who follow him, in the stubbornness of so many heretics who follow him, and in the manifold vices of the faithful who hold with him) has placed before his eyes—to humble Satan's pride and, as it were, to mock him—not a brave man adorned with much science, but rather a poor woman. She dared to challenge him alone and raise a banner against him, openly recruiting people who could overcome him, trample him underfoot, and bring his strength to naught. Without doubt, God wished to prove how much he is capable of in these our times, in which so many thousands of people—partly with their erring understanding, partly with their vicious morals—attack his kingdom; he willed that through one woman, the understanding of many might be enlightened and the morals of many improved, whose number daily increases to compensate for the damage inflicted.

So it has also pleased him, in this age of the Church, to prove to us that his grace never grows old, and that the power of his Spirit is no weaker now than it was in the first blessed times. Indeed, he now works through weaker means (according to nature) than back then, performing the very same thing, or almost the very same thing, that he did then. For the life that your Reverences lead (which is the second miraculous sign) and the perfection to which your Mother has led you: what is it other than an image of the holiness that existed in the early Church? Truly, what we read in the histories of those times, we now see with our own eyes in your customs. Your life shows us in deed what was previously so little in use that people believed it was now only to be found in books and bare words. Indeed, what we marvel at when we read it, and what the flesh hardly wants to believe, we now see fulfilled in your Reverences and your companions. Therefore take these two lilies, polished completely clean, and shut them in a crystal vessel, firm without fire. Place them in a gentle sweat-bath <note>original: "Schweissbad"</note>, so the white lily will spread wide and embrace and enclose the red within itself. But because the red is of a fiery nature and finds help from the outward warmth, it lets its hot balsamic scent out into the coldness of the white. Through this they become at odds, for neither wants to yield <note>original: "cedieren"</note> or give way to the other. This is caused by their contrary qualities <note>original: "Contrariæ qualitates"</note>, as you well know. Both grow into the heavens, but are driven down again by the wind. This happens several times until they are weary, tired, and exhausted from the labor of ascending and descending, and must rest upon the earth.

But with us, alas, exactly the opposite has happened. Then it is no longer said, as the world-teachers and listeners say, "We cannot, we cannot, we cannot," but as Paul says, "I can do all things through Christ Jesus who strengthens me" <note>original Greek: "En dynamounti me"</note>. And the true, right Gospel is not letter, resonance or sound, word or wind, but a power (not of men, but) of God, for the salvation of believers.
